title: What if you boiled pasta on Mars?
caption:
Pasta would never cook on Mars. 🍝🔴

Mars' air is only about 0.6% as thick as Earth's (≈610 Pa). At that pressure water boils at about 0 °C: the pot bubbles hard and stays near freezing.

Pasta needs water at around 80 °C to soften. Making water boil at 80 °C takes roughly 80 times Mars' air pressure.

The fix is a pressure cooker: seal the steam in and the boiling point climbs back above 80 °C.

Would you eat Mars pasta? Yes or no 👇

Send this to the friend who'd pack spaghetti for Mars.

Follow @the.impossible.lab for more impossible science.

⚠️ Don't try this. A misused or faulty pressure cooker can burst and scald: always follow the manufacturer's instructions.

sources: https://wikiwand.com/en/Atmosphere_of_Mars (average surface pressure about 610 Pa, 0.6 % of Earth's)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_point (water triple point 611.657 Pa, 0.01 °C: at Mars' average pressure liquid water can only exist right at ~0 °C, so it boils near 0 °C)
https://physicsworld.com/a/how-to-cook-pasta-the-scientific-way/ (about 80 °C water is enough for pasta to cook; starch gelatinises above 60 °C, gluten sets at 70-80 °C)
Computed: saturation vapour pressure of water at 80 °C ≈ 47.4 kPa (steam tables) -> 47.4 / 0.61 ≈ 78× Mars' average pressure (≈80×); at 100 °C, 101.3 kPa ≈ 166×
